newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul stocks drop on labour jitters, weak factors.
newsitem.headline: Seoul stocks drop on labour jitters, weak factors.

text.p: South Korean stocks slid on Wednesday on investor fears that compromise over a controversial labour law would sap the nation's long-term industrial vigour.
Brokers said concern over poor market fundamentals had also soured sentiment.
What was viewed as a reversal by President Kim Young-sam from earlier plans to tame worker militancy could delay crucial restructuring of the economy, they said.
Many companies are saddled with high costs and low efficiency, hurting their international competitiveness.
"President Kim's concession dims prospects of a long-term economic recovery," said Jeon Jeong-tak, a broker at Hyundai Securities.
The composite stock index lost 11.60 points or 1.68 percent to close on Wednesday at 678.94.
On Tuesday President Kim conceded the new labour law had sparked public anxiety and hurt the economy, and he agreed to reopen parliamentary debate on the law.
Wildcat strikes erupted after the bill was rammed through parliament on December 26 and have cost the nation $3.33 billion in lost production, the Trade Ministry said.
Lost exports were put at $509 million.
Kim's about-face followed a decision by the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions to call off indefinite stoppages and limit industrial action to one day each week.
Brokers said market fundamentals, such as interest rates and the declining value of South Korea's currency, the won, have also emerged as factors affecting sentiment.
"Investors have began to worry about the damage the labour unrest has caused. In addition, weakening market fundamentals have dented sentiment," said Kim Heung-shik of Hyundai Securities.
Brokers said they expected a record trade deficit in January because of the labour trouble.
The trade deficit would exceed $3 billion in January, a record monthly shortfall, according to the Trade Ministry.
The deficit hit $20.38 billion last year, double the amount in 1995 and the outlook for this year is grim.

Semiconductors, which account for about 20 percent of South Korea's exports, are expected to suffer in 1997 from sagging world prices of memory chips due to global oversupply, analysts said on Wednesday.
Brokers also said a downward correction in South Korean stocks had been anticipated after the market rallied for a two-week period up until Monday.

They said customer deposits at brokerages began to fall on Monday after this year's high of 2.93 trillion won ($3.4 billion) and interest rates rose because of prospects of heavy new three-year corporate bond issues in February.
Yields for the bonds rose to 12.05 percent on Wednesday from Monday's 11.85 percent, brokers said.

Brokers said the yen's weakness against the dollar had also made South Korean products less competitive with Japanese goods in overseas markets. The yen dropped to 118.65 on Wednesday from 117.5 the previous day.
The local won's depreciation against the U.S. unit was also seen blocking inflows of foreign funds for stock investment.
"Foreign investors will lose interest in the stock market if the won falls further because of dwindling benefits of holding won-denominated equity," said Choo Hee-yup of Dongwon Securities.
The won slid to 854.40 per dollar at Wednesday's close from 852.80 on Tuesday and around 840 at the beginning of this year.
